title: Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules
summary: FCC preempts state rules that require AT&T to keep offering home phone service.
body: The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state's right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations. AT&T's status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory. AT&T wants to stop offering basic phone service to new customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027. The order released today granted AT&T's request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC's previous approval of AT&T's petition to discontinue service. AT&T had tried to achieve the same result in court, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California's rules in July. Read full article Comments

title: Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers
summary: Meta is “re-evaluating” 2030 sustainability goals. Will others follow?
body: Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers. The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.” “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report. title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
summary: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn't stay private.
body: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. title: Watching as a giant star swallowed its neighbor and exploded
summary: A recent brightening turned out to be from a star orbiting inside another.
body: In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act. In a new Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar said. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it's really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.” Shared envelopes Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to fricti…

summary: "We tend to have a lot of technical discussion and debate. That point will continue to be debated."
body: SpaceX's successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA's path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year. For SpaceX's purposes, Saturday's mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships. That should expedite SpaceX's deployment of its newest generation of Starlink Internet satellites. NASA, meanwhile, believes a higher launch cadence will lead to faster learning as SpaceX develops a deep space version of Starship to ferry astronaut crews to the surface of the Moon. Early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida. A second Starship factory is also under construction at Kennedy, joining SpaceX's existing SpaceX production line at Starbase, Texas. With two launch sites, SpaceX will have the pieces in place to take the next leap with Starship. Read full article Comments

title: Army delays detonating "catastrophically hazardous" lead azide amid fear, anger
summary: Modeling predicts plume of neurotoxic lead could reach up to 100 miles away.
body: In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army announced Thursday that it would delay a plan to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week. The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week. "Public communication is essential to public trust," Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday . title: Valve says it might have to raise the price of supply-limited Steam Machines
summary: "We don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price..."
body: When the Steam Machine first started shipping in June , Valve said it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn't secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost. Now, as the last of the initial batch of Steam Machine reservations are finally being fulfilled, Valve says those supply and cost issues will continue into the foreseeable future and may even require a price change. "We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels," Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday . "As a result we don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we'll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained." If Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good company. All three major console manufacturers instituted historically atypical price increases in 2025 , with additional price hikes happening this year. Read full article Comments

body: The US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration. But questions remain about whether the FAA's effort to modernize the national airspace system is being done with all the proper risk assessments and adequate agency oversight of the private contractors involved. The nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13. More than 12,000 flights were canceled on that day alone, with the number rising to more than 20,000 over the weekend as stranded travelers scrambled to find accommodations or alternative transportation. Some international flights were allowed to depart prior to the broader resumption of air traffic. Nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN . The world’s richest man has outlined ambitious plans to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips. SpaceX has said it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. title: Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US
summary: TP-Link's struggle illustrates how Trump admin wields control over device makers.
body: TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn't allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn't been able to obtain an exemption. The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security. While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold. Read full article Comments

title: MAHA PAC spent more on steak, luxury club than candidates, report shows
summary: Expert called MAHA's spending "pretty unusual" for a PAC.
body: In the wake of the Make America Healthy Again movement's midterm wipeout , a top leader suggested the heavy losses came down to being outspent by wealthier, more powerful rivals. But a Stat report on MAHA's own spending in the run-up to the election raises questions about whether the group's priority was ever winning elections in the first place. The dive into the financial documents reveals that the MAHA PAC, led by Tony Lyons, spent more on allies, boosters, meals, luxuries, and its affiliated nonprofit than it did on political candidates. The findings are in stark contrast to an announcement from Lyons in the spring that he was heading a $100 million fundraiser to boost MAHA's clout in the midterms . In reality, MAHA PAC took in $3.2 million. During the election cycle, the PAC spent more than $10.5 million, with over $7 million coming from money it had collected previously. Read full article Comments

title: Traumatized teens sue school, cops after Doritos bag triggers AI gun alert
summary: Lawsuit: Over 99% of school system’s AI gun alerts were false positives.
body: In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman. Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and canceled the alert, which notified not only other school officials but also the Baltimore County Police Department that no response was needed. The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t. Read full article Comments
